title: Two kinds of tag, and why releases need the heavier one
summary: A lightweight tag is a file containing a sha. An annotated tag is a real object with an author, a date and a message. Create both, look inside them, and see why only one belongs on a release.
mental_model: A lightweight tag is a branch that never moves. An annotated tag is an object in its own right — it has its own sha, points at the commit, and records who tagged it and why. Releases want the second.

steps.title: Make a lightweight tag
steps.why: No flags: git just writes a file under `refs/tags` containing the commit sha. It is exactly as much machinery as a branch, minus the ability to move.
steps.expect: The file's content is the commit sha, character for character.

steps.title: Make an annotated tag
steps.why: `-a` with a message creates a tag *object*: tagger, date, message, and a pointer to the commit. `git tag -n` shows the messages, which is what makes a tag list readable months later.
commands: git tag -a v1.1.0 -m "Release 1.1.0 — adds dosing calibration"

steps.title: Prove they are different kinds of thing
steps.why: `cat-file -t` reports the object type each tag name resolves to. The lightweight one is a commit; the annotated one is a tag object that in turn points at the commit.
steps.expect: commit, then tag, then the tag object's contents with a tagger line.

verify.label: the annotated tag is its own object
the lightweight tag resolves straight to the commit

steps.title: See who tagged and when
steps.why: The tagger identity and date live in the tag object. For an audit trail — 'who cut this release, on what day' — a lightweight tag records nothing at all.
steps.expect: A tagger date for v1.1.0 and blanks for quick-mark.

steps.title: Tag an older commit
steps.why: Tags are not limited to HEAD. Naming a commit retroactively is normal when you realise a release was never tagged — the tag records when you tagged it, the commit records when the code was written.

steps.title: Sort tags like versions, not like strings
steps.why: Alphabetical sorting puts v1.10.0 before v1.9.0. `--sort=v:refname` understands version numbers, which matters the moment your project reaches double digits.
steps.expect: Plain sort puts v1.10.0 before v1.9.0; the version sort gets it right.

steps.title: Clean up the throwaway
steps.why: `tag -d` deletes locally. Lightweight tags are fine for personal bookmarks, but leaving them in a shared repository confuses release tooling that expects annotated tags.

verify.label: the release tag is annotated
verify.hint: use git tag -a with a message for anything release-related

verify.label: an older commit was tagged retroactively
the throwaway lightweight tag was removed

pitfalls: `git describe` ignores lightweight tags unless you pass `--tags`. Release tooling built on describe silently skips them.
A lightweight tag records nothing about who made it. For anything auditable, always `-a`.
Tag names and branch names share a namespace in practice — a tag called `main` will confuse every command you run.
`git tag -s` signs a tag with GPG, and `git tag -v` verifies it. Distributions rely on this for release provenance.
cheatsheet: lightweight: a file holding a sha
annotated: a real object with author and message
